home.title: A private baby monitor for every device you own
home.og_title: Nestwatch: a private baby monitor for every device you own
home.description: Nestwatch turns phones, tablets and computers into a baby monitor. Sound and video go directly between your own devices, end-to-end encrypted. No account, no cloud, open source.

hero.title: A baby monitor that stays in your home.
hero.lead: Nestwatch turns the phones, tablets and computers you already own into a baby monitor. Sound and video travel directly from one of your devices to another, end-to-end encrypted. There is no account to make and no cloud in between.
hero.note: Listen in any browser, nothing to install. Apps for Linux, macOS, Windows and Android; iPhone and iPad are coming.
hero.shot_alt: Nestwatch listener on a computer: three station tiles. Nursery shows sound with a live camera view, Leo's room is quiet, Grandma's is reconnecting. A side panel shows the listening settings with a room-level chart and threshold.
hero.shot_caption: The listener on a computer, following three stations (design preview).

promise.heading: Private by design
promise.intro: A baby monitor hears and sees the most private room of your home. Nestwatch is built so that what it hears stays between your devices.

items.title: Your devices talk to each other
items.body: Stations and listeners connect directly on your home network or over a VPN you run yourself. There is no Nestwatch account and no server in the middle.

items.title: End-to-end encrypted
items.body: Every connection is encrypted and authenticated with the Noise Protocol Framework. Only devices you paired can hear, see or talk through a station.

items.title: Nothing collected
items.body: No analytics, no crash uploads, no update checks, no recordings. Audio and video are never stored, and logs never contain sound or pictures.

how.heading: How it works
how.intro: Any phone, tablet or computer can be a station or a listener. The browser can listen, and through the relay it can be the station too.

steps.title: Set up a station
body: Put a device near your child and choose This device watches. It listens to the room and shows its sound level in a ring. The screen can be dimmed to near-black while it keeps monitoring.

steps.title: Pair a listener
body: On the station, tap Pair a listener. Scan the QR code, open the link, or type the 10-character code. When pairing by code, both screens show the same number so you can check nobody is in between. Pairing stays open for at most 10 minutes.

steps.title: Listen, talk, look
body: The listener plays the room when there is sound, alerts you, lets you hold to talk, and opens the camera only when you ask. Paired devices reconnect on their own, without a code.

features.heading: Everything a baby monitor needs, nothing it should not do

items.title: Sound activation with your threshold
items.body: The station sends audio only while the room is louder than the threshold you choose, with a short pre-roll so the start of a cry is never cut off. A chart of the last minute of room level helps you place the threshold just above the background noise. Prefer to hear everything? Switch to always on.

items.title: Talk-back
items.body: Hold to talk through the station's speaker. One listener talks at a time, and the others see who it is. The station shows when someone is talking.

items.title: Camera on demand
items.body: The camera is off whenever nobody is looking. Open the view from a listener and the station shows a clear indicator while it sends. A night-friendly grey image helps in a dark room. Sound always comes first; video adapts to the connection.

items.title: Several stations and listeners
items.body: Follow up to 8 stations at once, mixed into one calm view, with volume, mute and solo per station. A station serves up to 8 listeners, so both parents and the grandparents can listen.

items.title: Alerts that work while muted
items.body: Get an alert when a quiet room starts to sound, when a station has been unreachable for more than 20 seconds, and when a station's battery is low. Muting a station never mutes its alerts.

items.title: Calm at 3 a.m.
items.body: Warm, low-glare colours, a night and a day theme, and a dimmed station screen. Every status has a word next to its colour, never colour alone.

networks.heading: At home, and away over your own VPN

items.title: On your Wi-Fi
items.body: Listeners find stations on the home network by themselves (mDNS). Each tile shows which path it uses, and listeners reconnect after network changes, trying every address that worked before.

items.title: Over your own VPN
items.body: Already use Tailscale or WireGuard? Invitations include the station's VPN addresses and names, and you can type an address by hand. Listen from the grandparents' house without any Nestwatch server.

relay.heading: For difficult networks: an optional relay
relay.intro: Some networks block direct connections: mobile data behind carrier-grade NAT, guest Wi-Fi that isolates devices, firewalls that only allow HTTPS. For those, Nestwatch is getting an optional relay server that helps two devices find each other, tries to open a direct path between them and, only when that fails, forwards the encrypted stream. It is off until you turn it on, and you can run your own.
relay.can_heading: What a relay operator could see
can: that a station is online, and its public IP address
which IP addresses connect to it, and when
how many bytes flow, which can hint at when there is sound (choose always-on listening on relayed connections to hide this)
relay.cannot_heading: What it cannot see or do
cannot: hear audio, see video or read control messages: they are encrypted end to end between your devices
learn device names, pairing codes or keys; invitations never pass through it
pretend to be your station or alter traffic: the devices' own handshake would fail

cta.heading: Try Nestwatch on the devices you have
cta.body: Free and open source. Use an old phone or laptop as the station, and listen on your phone from this website.

download.title: Download Nestwatch
download.lead: Install Nestwatch on two devices: one as the station near your child, one as the listener. Every native app can do both.
download.description: Download Nestwatch for Linux (.deb, .rpm, .tar.gz), macOS (.dmg), Windows (.msi) and Android (.apk), or listen in the browser.
notice: Builds are attached to every release on GitHub Releases; the buttons below fetch the files of the latest release. Nestwatch is new: if a release has not been published yet, or a file is missing, build from source.

platforms.name: Linux
requirements: WebKitGTK 4.1 and GTK 3 (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04, Fedora 37 or newer)
PipeWire or PulseAudio with pulseaudio-utils for sound
notes: .deb for Debian and Ubuntu, .rpm for Fedora and other RPM-based distributions, .tar.gz for everything else: unpack it and run bin/nestwatch-desktop. The packages also contain nestwatch-station, a station without a window for a spare computer.

platforms.name: macOS
requirements: Apple silicon or Intel (one universal app)
notes: The app is not yet signed by Apple, so macOS blocks it the first time. Drag Nestwatch to Applications, open it once, then go to System Settings → Privacy & Security and choose Open Anyway. On macOS 14 and older you can instead Control-click the app and choose Open.

platforms.name: Windows
requirements: Microsoft Edge WebView2 (included in Windows 11 and current Windows 10)
notes: The installer is not yet code-signed, so SmartScreen may warn you. Choose More info → Run anyway if the file came from the release page and its checksum matches.

platforms.name: Android
platforms.roles: Station and listener, phone and tablet app.
notes: Open the downloaded file and allow your browser or file manager to install apps when asked. Releases built without the project's signing key carry a name that says so (…-testkey.apk); uninstall such a build before installing a properly signed one.
An Android station does not serve the browser listener yet; use a computer as the station for that.

platforms.name: Browser
platforms.roles: Listener, and station through the relay. Nothing to install: the easiest way to start.
requirements: Chrome or Edge 113, Firefox 128, Safari 17 or newer
notes: Open the web app on this site on any phone, tablet or computer and pair it with your station. It connects through the relay, so it works from anywhere, and talk-back works because the site uses HTTPS. Switch on Reachable through a relay server on the station.
At home you can also open the web address a computer station shows on its pairing screen; that copy is served by the station itself and needs no relay.

The web app on this site can also be the station: choose Use this device as a station. It is reachable through the relay only, and its tab must stay open and visible, because phones pause tabs in the background. For a whole night, a phone or computer with the Nestwatch app makes the more reliable station.

platforms.name: iPhone and iPad
notes: The iOS app is planned on the same core as the other apps and is not available yet.

source.heading: Build from source
body: Nestwatch is written in Rust. With a current Rust toolchain (and on Linux the WebKitGTK development packages listed in apps/desktop):
source.code:
git clone https://github.com/jeroentrappers/nestwatch
cd nestwatch
apps/web/build.sh                         # browser listener the station serves
cargo run --release -p nestwatch-desktop  # desktop app

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lead: The short version: what Nestwatch hears and sees goes from your station to your listeners and nowhere else.
privacy.description: How Nestwatch keeps your home private: no cloud, no account, end-to-end encryption, no recordings, and exactly what an optional relay server can and cannot see.

sections.heading: In plain words
list: No account, no cloud. Nestwatch has no sign-up and no company server that your audio or video passes through.
Only your devices. The apps talk only to your own devices, plus a relay server if, and only if, you turn one on.
Encrypted end to end. Everything between a station and a listener is encrypted and authenticated, also on your own Wi-Fi.
No recordings. Nestwatch never records audio or video, and keeps no history of either.
No tracking. No analytics, no advertising, no crash reports, no update checks, no fonts or scripts loaded from the internet.

sections.heading: Who can listen
body: A listener can only follow a station after you paired them. Pairing works only while you have the pairing screen open on the station: at most 10 minutes, up to 8 devices, and after 5 wrong codes it closes.
When you pair by code, both devices show the same number. If the numbers differ, someone may be in between: choose Different and try again.
Every listener has its own key. On the station you see every trusted listener and can remove one at any time; it is disconnected immediately and refused afterwards, without affecting the others.

sections.heading: How it is protected
body: Connections use the Noise Protocol Framework: both devices prove who they are with their own keys, every session gets fresh keys, and messages that are changed, replayed or reordered end the session.

Keys stay on the device that made them, in the system's key store where there is one (Android Keystore, macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, the Secret Service on Linux). They are never exported, logged or put in backups. A new phone means pairing again.

sections.heading: Camera and microphone
body: The station's camera starts only when a listener opens the camera view, and stops when the last one closes it. While it sends, the station shows an unmistakable indicator, and it always shows how many listeners are connected and whether someone is talking.
Apps ask for microphone and camera permission only when a feature first needs it, and explain why. You can switch the camera and talk-back off entirely on a station.

sections.heading: The browser listener
body: The browser listener is served by your own station and loads nothing from anywhere else. Its key and settings stay in that browser's storage for the station's address. Over plain HTTP the conversation is still end-to-end encrypted; the station's HTTPS address also protects the app itself and is needed for talk-back. Check that the certificate fingerprint matches the one the station shows.

sections.heading: If you turn on a relay
body: The optional relay is for networks where your devices cannot reach each other directly. It is off by default; a station uses it only after you enable it and choose the server. The project plans to run one at nestwatch.appmire.be, and you can run your own.

head: The relay operator
rows: That a station is online; its public IP address; which IP addresses connect to it and when; how many bytes flow.
Audio, video, control messages, device names, pairing codes or keys. Everything after the first few bytes is encrypted between your devices, and invitations never pass through the server.
Pretend to be your station, or change what is sent: the devices' handshake fails and the session closes.

after: Byte counts can reveal when there is sound, because sound activation sends audio only then. On relayed connections you can choose always-on listening to hide this. Relayed devices keep trying to switch to a direct path. The server keeps no recordings, does not log mailbox IDs or contents, and keeps IP addresses only as long as abuse protection needs, at most 24 hours.

sections.heading: This website
body: This site is plain static pages. It sets no cookies, has no analytics or trackers, and loads no fonts or scripts from other servers. The only thing it remembers is your choice of night or day theme, stored in your own browser.

sections.heading: The details
body: The full threat model and rules are in the specifications: security.md and rendezvous.md §7.

self-hosting.title: Run your own relay
self-hosting.lead: The relay server is a single program with no database. If you have a small Linux server with a domain name, you can run your own and point your devices at it.
self-hosting.description: How to self-host the optional Nestwatch relay server: a single binary behind nginx or Caddy, HTTPS with WebSocket on /nwr/1, UDP 3478, and a systemd unit.

sections.heading: Status
body: The relay server (nestwatch-server) and relay support in the apps are being finalized. This page describes the planned deployment so you can prepare; details such as option names may still change. The full, current guide is docs/self-hosting.md.

sections.heading: What it does
body: The server helps a listener reach a station without knowing its address, helps both open a direct connection through their routers, and forwards the encrypted stream when no direct path works. It only ever sees encrypted data: the devices' own handshake runs end to end through it. The same HTTPS address can host this website and the browser listener.

sections.heading: What you need
list: A Linux server reachable from the internet, with a domain name
A reverse proxy for HTTPS (nginx or Caddy) that passes WebSocket upgrades on /nwr/1
Open firewall ports: TCP 443 (HTTPS) and UDP 3478 (address discovery for direct connections)
One directory for state (the server keeps hashed mailbox secrets and transfer counters there); no database

sections.heading: Setup in short
list: Download nestwatch-server-linux-x86_64 from the latest release (when available) and install it as /usr/local/bin/nestwatch-server.
Create a system user and a state directory, for example /var/lib/nestwatch-server.
Run it with systemd: it listens on a local HTTP port for the reverse proxy and directly on UDP 3478.

Configure nginx or Caddy for your domain: forward /nwr/1 to that local port with WebSocket upgrades, and serve the static website and browser listener (nestwatch-site.tar.gz, nestwatch-web.tar.gz) for everything else.
On each station, turn on Reachable through a relay server and enter your server's address, for example https://relay.example.org.
after: Configuration for nginx, the systemd unit and the firewall rules are in docs/self-hosting.md.

sections.heading: Limits and logging
body: The server limits how much one station and one IP address can use (concurrent connections, a rate per connection and a monthly transfer budget), so one household cannot exhaust it. It logs only totals, never contents, and keeps IP addresses only as long as abuse protection needs, at most 24 hours.

about.title: Open source
about.lead: Nestwatch is free software. You can read every line, build it yourself, and share it.
about.description: Nestwatch is open source under the GNU AGPL v3.0 or later: a Rust core with Dioxus desktop apps, a wasm browser listener and a Jetpack Compose Android app.

sections.heading: License
body: Nestwatch is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 or later. You may use, study, change and share it; if you distribute a changed version or run it as a service for others, you share your changes under the same license.

The AGPL conflicts with Apple App Store rules. Before an iOS release, the copyright holder intends to grant an explicit additional permission for app-store distribution, or to distribute iOS builds another way.

sections.heading: What is inside

head: Part
Built with
State
rows: Desktop apps for Linux, macOS, Windows
Kotlin and Jetpack Compose on the Rust core (UniFFI)

after: The behaviour of every app comes from one set of specifications: the product requirements, the wire protocol, the security model and the platform rules. Code follows the specs, and changes to behaviour go through the specs first.

sections.heading: Contributing
list: Report bugs and ideas in GitHub Issues. Please never attach recordings or pictures of your home.
Read the specs before changing behaviour; requirements carry stable IDs such as FR-PAIR-3 that tests and issues refer to.
Pull requests are checked with rustfmt, clippy and the tests, and every app is built on Linux, macOS, Windows and Android.
Translations are welcome: the website keeps every string in one file per language.

sections.heading: Why Nestwatch
body: Many connected baby monitors send the sound of your child's room through a company's servers, and depend on that company to keep working. Nestwatch uses the devices you already have, keeps everything between them, and is built in the open so that it can be checked and keep working.

faq.title: Questions and answers
faq.description: Answers to common questions about Nestwatch: internet access, number of devices, battery, the browser listener, iPhone support and safety.

a: No. On your home network the station and listeners talk directly to each other. To listen from somewhere else, connect your devices with your own VPN such as Tailscale or WireGuard. An optional relay server for networks where that is not possible is in development.

items.q: Do I need to create an account?
a: No. There are no accounts. Devices trust each other after you pair them once.

items.q: How many devices can I use?
a: A station serves up to 8 listeners, and a listener can follow up to 8 stations at the same time, for example one per child's room.

items.q: Can I use an old phone or laptop as the station?
a: Yes, that is what Nestwatch is for. Keep it on the charger: a station listens all the time. Android stations keep running with the screen off; computers stay awake while a station runs (the display may still turn off).

items.q: Will it wake me for every little sound?
a: You choose. With sound activation, the station sends audio only while the room is louder than your threshold; a chart of the last minute shows where the background noise is. You can also listen all the time and still get an alert when sound starts.

items.q: Can I listen in a web browser?
a: Yes. Open the web app on this site on any computer, tablet or phone, and pair it with a station that has the relay switched on. At home you can also use the web address a computer station shows when you pair; it is served by the station itself.

The browser can be the station as well: in the web app on this site, choose Use this device as a station. It is reachable through the relay only and keeps its keys in that browser; keep the tab open and visible while it watches.
Not yet. The iPhone and iPad app is planned. Until then, an iPhone can listen in Safari to a computer that runs the station.
No. The camera starts only while a listener has the camera view open, and the station shows that it is on. You can turn the camera off completely in the station settings.
No. Nestwatch has no recording or history. Sound and pictures are only played live on your listeners.

items.q: Does it check my baby's breathing or health?
a: No. Nestwatch is not a medical device and does not replace supervision. It lets you hear, see and talk to the room, nothing more.
Nothing. Nestwatch is free and open source software under the GNU AGPL.
